text:
Today, Avnos is introducing the Avnos HDAC™ Module, the company’s first standardized, factory-built product family.

Specialized in infrastructure-scale Hybrid Direct Air Capture (HDAC™) technology, Avnos is now entering a new stage of operations in which its standardized HDAC module moves into commercial manufacturing, having been tested and deemed as ready for deployment.

With this announcement, the company is unveiling a standardized, factory-built product line created through a repeatable manufacturing process that will enable Avnos to serve an even wider range of customers.

This production breakthrough has also helped unlock a major reduction in Direct Air Capture capital costs, with the company expecting to lower them further as new module variants come to market.

Powered by a single technology platform, the Avnos HDAC Module launches with three core infrastructure applications: data centers, carbon storage, and E-fuels.

The different applications of the Avnos HDAC™ Module

The Avnos HDAC Data Center Modules harness low-grade waste heat to provide cooling support, produce clean water on-site, and remove carbon dioxide emissions from the atmosphere, all through one platform while using resources the facility already has.

The Carbon Storage HDAC Modules capture carbon dioxide emissions directly from the atmosphere to deliver a clean and high-purity steam of CO2 stream for permanent geologic storage.

This innovation is already being deployed, with the first Avnos HDAC Carbon Storage Modules planned for delivery to Project Cedar, the company’s largest deployment to date. Cedar will deploy four modules capable of capturing 3,000 tonnes of CO2 and producing more than 6,000 tonnes of clean water on an annual basis.

Relevant: “HDAC Is Built For The Data Center Era” – Will Kain, Avnos Founder & CEO

Avnos highlights that these factory-built modules are designed for flexible and rapid installation near Class VI wells and regional carbon storage hubs.

The Avnos HDAC eFuels Modules serve to supply high-purity atmospheric CO2 and clean water as feedstocks for the production of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), methanol, and other synthesis pathways, providing two critical inputs from a single platform.

Will Kain, founder and CEO of Avnos, commented, “Moving to factory-built HDAC Modules gives us the foundation to grow with our customers, lower the cost of delivering infrastructure, and deploy at a significantly greater scale.”

Looking ahead, the company plans further configurations as the platform expands.

title: Aviation's climate plan is missing the point - Fast Company
description:
In an earlier Fast Company Impact Council article, I argued that not all “green” jet fuel is equal.
Net-zero commitments linked to aviation must also account for the resilience of the fuel supply behind them.
How exposed are we to single points of failure in global energy supply?
Long-term commitments from airlines, logistics companies, and corporate buyers can help unlock investment in facilities that turn local waste into local fuel.
FINAL THOUGHTS Aviation’s climate plan and its energy security plan should not be separate documents.
text:
Volatility is increasingly dominating boardroom discussions. Escalating conflict in the Middle East, shifting trade policies, and wider geopolitical tensions are sending repeated shocks through international markets. These disruptions are exposing the fragility of global supply chains and of the energy systems that keep them moving.

Aviation offers a clear example. Modern commerce depends on air networks to move essential cargo and connect people and businesses across borders. When geopolitical events threaten global oil supplies, jet fuel quickly becomes a critical vulnerability. The effects ripple across the economy: manufacturers face delays in receiving vital components, while retailers see high-value inventory held up far from its destination.

To reduce aviation’s environmental impact, the industry has developed sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF. Made from renewable feedstocks such as used cooking oil and agricultural waste, SAF can be used in existing aircraft and fuel infrastructure when blended with conventional jet fuel. Yet many corporate teams still see it primarily as a means of meeting climate targets.

That narrow framing overlooks a significant strategic opportunity. Producing renewable jet fuel from domestic waste and residue streams can strengthen economic resilience by diversifying fuel supplies. A more localized production model can reduce reliance on vulnerable international chokepoints while supporting a more distributed energy system. In this context, waste-based SAF is not only a climate solution; it can also help businesses and economies better withstand future geopolitical disruption.

FROM GREEN FUEL TO RESILIENCE

The climate case for SAF is familiar to industry specialists, though less so to many business leaders. Made from waste and renewable feedstocks, SAF can offer significantly lower lifecycle emissions than conventional jet fuel. It is also expected to play a central role in aviation’s pathway to net zero.

But SAF is more than a climate solution. When produced from domestic waste and residue streams, it can perform like conventional jet fuel while diversifying a region’s energy supply and retaining local supply. That combination—drop-in compatibility and local production—should matter to boards as much as it does to sustainability teams.

In an earlier Fast Company Impact Council article, I argued that not all “green” jet fuel is equal. Credible SAF should meet three tests: It should use genuine waste or residue feedstocks, deliver verified lifecycle emissions reductions, and create circular local benefits.

Today, a fourth test is needed: Does this fuel reduce exposure to global supply shocks by building local-to-local energy systems?

A LOCAL-TO-LOCAL MODEL

Through this lens, waste-based SAF becomes both a climate tool and an energy security asset.

A resilient local-to-local model rests on three principles:

1. Local feedstock: Agricultural residues, used cooking oil, and some waste streams are available in nearly every region. Converting them into certified SAF can create domestic fuel resources without competing with food production or requiring additional land.

2. Regional production: Locating conversion facilities near feedstock sources and aviation hubs can reduce dependence on imported jet fuel and distant refineries. It also builds regional industrial capability that is less exposed to disruption than long, single-route supply chains.

3. Circular co-benefits: Converting waste into fuel can reduce local pollution, relieve landfill pressure, and create economic opportunities for farmers, collectors, and small businesses. Those benefits make the transition more durable than one based solely on imported fuel.

Waste-to-fuel systems can operate at scale, even within complex regional and global supply chains. One example is EcoCeres’ work in Hong Kong where we developed processes that convert used cooking oil, agricultural waste, and other residues into renewable fuels at industrial scale, including through a large-scale facility in mainland China.

The underlying logic applies everywhere. Regions that depend heavily on imported fossil jet fuel can reduce that exposure by investing in waste-based SAF capacity and the infrastructure needed to bring fuel from local producers to local airports.

WHY LEADERS SHOULD CARE

For many business leaders, SAF remains a technical issue for airline operations teams and sustainability specialists. It represents a small share of today’s jet-fuel supply and usually costs more than conventional fuel. As a result, it does not yet feature prominently in boardroom discussions about geopolitical risk.

advertisement

This separation is risky. Net-zero commitments linked to aviation must also account for the resilience of the fuel supply behind them. A climate strategy that depends on fuel unavailable during a crisis is not a complete resilience strategy.

Boards and ESG teams should ask:

What is the emissions profile of the fuels we rely on?

How exposed are we to single points of failure in global energy supply?

If the answer to the second question is “highly exposed,” SAF belongs at the center of the energy security conversation, not at the edge of a climate plan.

Conversations are only the starting point. Leaders can use these three strategies for moving energy security discussions forward.

1. Build energy security into climate strategies. Assess low-carbon fuels not only by their emissions reductions, but also by their ability to diversify supply and reduce exposure to geopolitical shocks.

2. Support regional, waste-based SAF projects through procurement. Long-term commitments from airlines, logistics companies, and corporate buyers can help unlock investment in facilities that turn local waste into local fuel.

3. Work with policymakers to build resilient infrastructure. That means supporting systems for feedstock collection, production, certification, and distribution, alongside regulations that reward verified lifecycle performance.

FINAL THOUGHTS

Aviation’s climate plan and its energy security plan should not be separate documents. They should be one and the same.

Treating waste-based SAF as a resilience tool, built on local resources, regional production, and circular value chains, can help protect both the climate and the global economy from the next fuel shock.

description:

text:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia’s aerospace industry is strengthening its position in the regional supply chain as local companies expand into higher-value manufacturing, maintenance and engineering services.

Malaysia is currently home to more than 250 aerospace companies, generating RM32.5bil in industry revenue and employing over 30,000 skilled workers, according to the Malaysian Investment Development Authority (MIDA).

The country has developed capabilities spanning research and development, engineering and design, manufacturing, maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO), as well as talent development.

Over the past five years, Malaysia approved 30 aerospace investment projects worth RM2.7bil, which are expected to create more than 2,600 high-value jobs across aerospace manufacturing, MRO, engineering and related services.

MIDA chief executive officer Datuk Sikh Shamsul Ibrahim Sikh Abdul Majid said the next phase of the industry’s development would involve building more local champions capable of competing internationally and moving into higher-value segments of the aerospace supply chain.

“This ambition is fully aligned with the Malaysian Aerospace Industry Blueprint 2030, which envisions Malaysia as the leading aerospace nation in Southeast Asia and an integral part of the global aerospace industry,” he said.

Among the Malaysian companies expanding their aerospace presence is Pecca Aviation Services Sdn Bhd, which has moved into aircraft seat covers and soft furnishings after building its manufacturing base in the automotive leather upholstery industry.

The company became the first Malaysian company to obtain European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) Production Organisation Approval Part 21G under C2 certification.

The approval allows Pecca Aviation to manufacture, repair, refurbish and install aircraft seat covers and soft furnishings for EASA-compliant aircraft worldwide.

"Achieving EASA certification placed us alongside established aviation MRO players in Europe and the United States while opening new opportunities to compete internationally.

“More importantly, it demonstrated that a Malaysian company can meet one of the world's highest aviation manufacturing standards," Pecca Aviation executive director Hugo Teoh said.

The company recently signed a memorandum of understanding with Myanmar Airways International at the MyAERO Summit 2026 as part of efforts to expand its regional presence.

It is also collaborating with Politeknik Banting and Universiti Tun Hussein Onn Malaysia to develop aerospace talent.

Meanwhile, Asia Digital Engineering (ADE) has expanded its MRO operations at Kuala Lumpur International Airport Terminal 2 from a single maintenance line into a 16-line facility serving AirAsia and international customers, including Air France.

ADE has also developed digital platforms including AEROTRADE and ELEVADE, which incorporate predictive maintenance, artificial intelligence, aircraft health monitoring and workforce optimisation.

ADE chief executive officer Mahesh Kumar said Malaysia had an opportunity to compete for aerospace business based on quality, innovation and operational capabilities rather than cost alone.

The company has also established a Maintenance Training Organisation to train engineers and technicians in internationally recognised qualifications and digital competencies.

Malaysia is targeting further expansion in the aerospace industry under the Malaysian Aerospace Industry Blueprint 2030 and New Industrial Master Plan 2030.

By 2030, the aerospace sector is projected to generate RM20.4bil in MRO revenue, RM21.2bil from aero-manufacturing and RM13.6bil from engineering and design services.

The country's aerospace ecosystem is also expanding into sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

PETRONAS delivered Malaysia’s first locally blended, ISCC-certified SAF to Kuala Lumpur International Airport in September 2025, while projects including EcoCeres’ biorefinery in Johor and the planned PETRONAS-Eni-Euglena facility in Pengerang are expected to increase domestic SAF production capacity.

MIDA said the growth of Malaysian aerospace companies would help strengthen domestic supply chains, generate high-value employment and increase the country's participation in the global aerospace value chain.

title: Emerson Selected for SkyNRG Sustainable Aviation Fuel Plant in Netherlands
description:

The plant will convert residual fats and greases into a “drop-in” sustainable aviation fuel that can be blended with conventional jet fuel without requiring modifications to aircraft or existing fuelling infrastructure.
The systems will support process control, safety shutdown functions and fire and gas detection across the facility.
“Developing Europe’s first dedicated sustainable aviation fuel facility is a major step in scaling SAF production and supporting aviation decarbonization,” said Bart Rosendaal, Site Director of DSL-01 at SkyNRG.

text:
Emerson has been selected by Technip Energies to provide automation technologies for SkyNRG’s sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) plant currently under construction in Delfzijl, Netherlands. The facility is expected to produce approximately 100,000 tonnes of SAF annually once fully operational in 2028.

The plant will convert residual fats and greases into a “drop-in” sustainable aviation fuel that can be blended with conventional jet fuel without requiring modifications to aircraft or existing fuelling infrastructure. The project is intended to contribute to the Netherlands’ efforts to meet European Union SAF requirements and support the objectives of the ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation.

Under the regulation, jet fuel supplied at EU airports is required to contain at least 2% SAF from 2025, with the requirement scheduled to increase progressively to 70% by 2050. The development of dedicated SAF production capacity is expected to support the aviation sector’s transition towards lower-carbon fuels.

Emerson will provide its DeltaV integrated control and safety system (ICSS), incorporating the DeltaV Distributed Control System and DeltaV Safety Instrumented System. The systems will support process control, safety shutdown functions and fire and gas detection across the facility.

AMS Device Manager software will provide access to field device information, equipment health insights and diagnostics. The technology is designed to support commissioning activities and ongoing maintenance by providing operators and maintenance teams with greater visibility into device performance.

The automation systems will manage the plant’s process units, including the hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids (HEFA) process used to produce SAF, an advanced feedstock pre-treatment unit and an on-site hydrogen plant. The hydrogen facility will use Technip Energies’ proprietary high-efficiency steam methane reforming technology.

Emerson will also provide end-to-end project services and integrate the integrated control and safety system with the plant’s modular production units. DeltaV Electronic Marshalling with distributed CHARMs will be used to simplify field wiring infrastructure, with the aim of reducing associated costs and providing greater flexibility to accommodate late-stage engineering and design changes.

“Developing Europe’s first dedicated sustainable aviation fuel facility is a major step in scaling SAF production and supporting aviation decarbonization,” said Bart Rosendaal, Site Director of DSL-01 at SkyNRG. “Working with experienced partners like Technip Energies and Emerson helps ensure we can deliver a safe, reliable and future-ready plant from day one.”

Nathan Pettus, President of Emerson’s Process Systems and Solutions business, said, “Projects such as SkyNRG’s SAF facility represent the future of energy and sustainable fuels. With complex, first-of-a-kind plants, early engineering alignment and a fully integrated automation architecture are key to delivering predictable project outcomes and consistent operational performance over the long term.”

Founded in 1890, Emerson has evolved from an electric motor manufacturer into a multinational corporation serving industrial, commercial, and residential markets. It delivers products such as process control systems, measurement instruments, industrial valves, and industrial software used in sectors like energy, chemicals, life sciences, and manufacturing. Emerson’s mission is to solve complex industrial challenges through digital transformation and intelligent automation. Its solutions help companies reduce energy use, increase productivity, enhance safety, and achieve sustainability goals.

text:
Britain’s Climate Change Committee (CCC) said that there is no credible pathway for Heathrow Airport’s expansion under current policies. At the same time, the UK can still meet its 2050 net-zero target unless airlines are made fully responsible for their emissions. The advice came at the government’s request, after Labor backed a £64 billion third runway at Heathrow in 2025 on economic-growth grounds.

CCC Chair Nigel Topping said the government cannot expand Heathrow without requiring the aviation sector to clean up its emissions, and the committee urged legislation that would force airlines to address all emissions by 2050 through sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) or engineered carbon removal. SAF still makes up less than 1% of global jet fuel use and remains far costlier than conventional fuel, while global carbon removals total under 2 million metric tons to date.

The CCC also called for a 25-year net-zero aviation strategy and contingency planning in case key technologies underdeliver. The Department for Transport said it will review the advice.

Featured ESG Tool of the Week:

Klimado – Navigating climate complexity just got easier. Klimado offers a user-friendly platform for tracking local and global environmental shifts, making it an essential tool for climate-aware individuals and organizations.

Indonesia wildfires choke Borneo, increasing respiratory illness cases

Indonesia is battling its worst wildfires in 11 years, worsened by a “super El Niño” which has driven up temperatures and drought across Borneo and Sumatra. According to health ministry data, more than 12.5 million people across seven provinces have been exposed to the resulting haze, with respiratory illness cases more than doubling to 113,336 by September 9, up from 50,891 on September 1.

In West Kalimantan’s capital, Pontianak, residents describe worsening breathing problems, and volunteers are distributing oxygen cylinders door-to-door through a campaign called “Rumah Oksigen” (Oxygen House). Air quality has also deteriorated in neighboring Singapore and Malaysia due to transboundary smog.

The EU’s Copernicus climate monitoring service reported Indonesia’s emissions hit 19.7 million metric tons in the week to September 7 — more than a third of the global total. Fires have burned through 202,000 hectares this year, with environmental group YKAN estimating 600,000 more hectares damaged in August alone.

Isometric raises $50 million as ICE backs carbon certification

Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), operator of the New York Stock Exchange, has joined Isometric’s Series A round, bringing it to $50 million and pushing the certification platform’s total funding to $75 million since its seed round.

Isometric uses an AI-powered platform, Certify, alongside independent verifiers to validate sustainability claims, cutting certification timelines from months to hours, the company says. Originally built around carbon removal, Isometric has been contracted to certify more than 16 million tonnes, making it the largest certifier globally by contracted volume. Its scope has since expanded into industrial emissions, energy, fuels and materials, with over 200 projects now using its infrastructure, including customers like Microsoft, Anglo American, Boeing and JPMorgan Chase.

ICE brings decades of experience running financial, energy, and environmental markets. The partnership signals a broader shift: as capital flows into data centers, clean energy, and industrial decarbonisation, verified sustainability data is becoming financial infrastructure in its own right.

NYC’s 9/11 transparency portal reveals officials concealed air quality risks

New York City has released a public portal containing over 170,000 pages of documents on post-9/11 environmental hazards. This reveals what city officials allegedly knew about toxic air quality and health risks near Ground Zero. Launched September 8 under Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration, the portal includes contamination records, internal memos, and inter-agency correspondence showing officials may have prematurely told residents and workers it was safe to return, exposing them to asbestos and other toxins.

The release settles a multi-year lawsuit by 9/11 Health Watch, which sought the “Harding Memo”—an internal 2001 warning to then-Deputy Mayor Robert Harding estimating up to 10,000 potential legal claims tied to hazardous air exposure. A May court ruling called the city’s earlier refusal to release records “arbitrary and capricious,” prompting the settlement.

Mamdani said the city owes survivors and first responders “transparency and accountability” and confirmed that $34 million was allocated for the portal, which will continue to be updated as more documents are reviewed.

title: Cathay welcomes new Five-Year Plan to strengthen international aviation hub status
description:
Cathay welcomed the government's initiatives outlined in the First Five-Year Plan and the Policy Address to enhance Hong Kong’s international aviation hub status, the carrier said in a statement on Wednesday.
"As the city’s home hub carrier, we have already committed around HK$150 billion in investments into our fleet, cabin and lounge products, and digital innovation," chief executive officer Ronald Lam Siu-por said.
Meanwhile, Cathay pledged to support measures to enhance collaboration and intermodal connectivity across the Greater Bay Area for both travel and cargo transport.
Furthermore, Cathay stated that it is also encouraged by the government's continued focus on developing an internationally competitive sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) value chain in Hong Kong and the wider GBA.
"A well-designed mandatory SAF mechanism will strengthen the city’s position as a leading aviation hub while supporting the growth of SAF production and uptake by providing long-term demand certainty," the carrier stated.

The latest blueprint includes expanding connectivity through new routes and increased frequencies, strengthening collaboration and intermodal transportation across the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA), and promoting the development of the sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) value chain in the region.

"As the city’s home hub carrier, we have already committed around HK$150 billion in investments into our fleet, cabin and lounge products, and digital innovation," chief executive officer Ronald Lam Siu-por said.

title: Bayer and Neste form partnership to scale US winter canola for biofuels production
description:
The initiative would strengthen the oilseed supply potential of lower carbon-intensity feedstocks to meet growing global demand for biofuels such as renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), the companies said on 9 September.

text:
STOCKHOLM, Sept. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Google has entered into an agreement with Stegra for the purchase of environmental attribute certificates (EACs) connected to Stegra's steel production in Boden, Sweden. These EACs help scale global supply for near-zero emission steel.

The agreement covers EACs for a volume of up to 91.000 tonnes of steel for the first year, with an ambition to add more volumes over the length of the agreement.

"Decarbonizing the most challenging sectors requires every tool in our toolbox. Alongside physical procurement, certificates are another vital mechanism. Having proven this model with clean electricity and expanded it to other areas like sustainable aviation fuel, we see green steel EACs as another promising lever to address industrial emissions and scale the clean technologies of the future," says Adam Elman, Director of Sustainability for Google in Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

With these EACs, Google can address the steel-related emissions from its own operations, including the construction of datacenters. Google also contributes to generating increased cash flow to Stegra's early years of operations, and the ramp-up of production.

"There are some players globally that can help move markets towards decarbonized products in an impactful way. Google is naturally one such player. Beyond the call to action to increase the supply of sustainably produced steel, we are also grateful that the team at Google chose to work with Stegra and support our first years of operations in this way," says Henrik Henriksson, CEO Stegra.

Near-zero emission steel will initially be available at limited volumes and in few locations. Purchasing environmental attributes enables committed buyers to address their steel-related emissions, even when direct procurement of the physical product is challenging, due to factors like geographical separation or value chain separation.

This is also a mechanism that can support the scaling and financing of new industrial companies in clean tech, and the investment in new sustainable technologies.

This is made possible by decoupling the environmental attributes from the physical product, also known as "book and claim". The physical steel is delivered as steel without the environmental attributes, which are delivered separately through EACs.

Stegra applies book and claim to the non-prime steel it produces. Every steel mill produces some non-prime steel, but when you start a new steel mill, the share of non-prime steel is larger. This steel is made in the same process as the rest of the production, which in Stegra's case is with green hydrogen and renewable electricity. To ensure there is no double counting of emission avoidance, the buyer of the physical steel will be obliged to commit to not make any green claims.

title: Luxury flights to Antarctica to run on used cooking oil fuel
description:
White Desert operates one flight a week from Cape Town to Antarctica during the November-to-February season.
Its first flight using Sasol’s fuel is expected to take place in November on an Airbus A340-600, Reuters reported.
It is made from materials such as used cooking oil rather than crude oil and can be blended with regular aviation fuel.
White Desert previously sourced SAF from Europe.
The fuel can cost two to three times more than conventional aviation fuel.
text: Travellers flying from Cape Town to Antarctica will soon be able to make the journey on fuel partly made from used cooking oil.Sasol, a South African company that produces fuels and chemicals, has started supplying sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) to White Desert, a luxury tourism operator that organises trips to the continent, Bloomberg and Reuters reported. White Desert operates one flight a week from Cape Town to Antarctica during the November-to-February season. Its first flight using Sasol’s fuel is expected to take place in November on an Airbus A340-600, Reuters reported. The company’s packages include one-day trips priced at USD16,500 and seven-day journeys costing up to USD120,000. Activities include glacier excursions, visits to Antarctica’s Blue Rivers and champagne gatherings in an ice bar, according to information cited by Bloomberg. The deal comes as tourism to Antarctica expands and operators face pressure to reduce the environmental impact of taking visitors to one of the world’s most sensitive regions. SAF is an alternative to conventional jet fuel. It is made from materials such as used cooking oil rather than crude oil and can be blended with regular aviation fuel. The fuel does not eliminate emissions from flying, but it can help reduce the carbon impact of air travel. Aviation accounts for about 2 per cent of global carbon dioxide emissions and 12 per cent of emissions from transport, according to the US Department of Energy. White Desert previously sourced SAF from Europe. It switched to Sasol after the company’s fuel received certification, Reuters reported. Sasol produces the fuel at its Natref refinery. The company is the world’s biggest producer of fuels and chemicals from coal and one of South Africa’s biggest greenhouse-gas emitters. “This we see as a very first practical commercial step,” Danie Cronje, Sasol’s senior vice president for business building, strategy and technology, told Bloomberg. Sasol can currently produce up to 2 million litres of SAF a year at Natref. It plans to increase production to about 16 million litres in 2027 and up to 100 million litres by 2030, Reuters reported. SAF accounted for about 0.6 per cent of global jet-fuel demand last year, according to BloombergNEF analysts. The fuel can cost two to three times more than conventional aviation fuel. Sasol said it has received interest from other potential customers and is working on additional commercial agreements.

text:
The first phase of the Saldanha Bay facility will receive a US$100 million equity commitment from Phelan Green Group.

Phase one is expected to produce 35,000 tonnes of e SAF a year, with construction scheduled to begin in the first quarter of 2027.

The project is the first of six priority green hydrogen initiatives supported by South Africa to reach a final investment decision.

Phelan Green Group has taken a final investment decision on the first phase of its planned electro sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) facility at Saldanha Bay in South Africa.

South African President Cyril Ramaphosa announced the decision at the African Green Hydrogen Summit 2026. The development marks the transition of the project from planning to implementation and makes it the first of six priority green hydrogen projects supported by the national programme to reach this stage.

The first phase will be supported by a US$100 million equity commitment from Phelan Green Group. The full development, which will be delivered in several phases, is expected to cost R47 billion, equivalent to about US$2.9 billion.

The first phase is designed to produce 35,000 tonnes of e SAF annually. Later phases are expected to increase total production capacity to 140,000 tonnes a year.

Construction at the Saldanha Bay site is scheduled to begin in the first quarter of 2027. The project is targeting its first commercial exports in the first quarter of 2029.

The facility will use Honeywell UOP’s Unicracking process together with Johnson Matthey’s HyCOgen and FT CANS technologies. The integrated system will combine green hydrogen with captured carbon dioxide to produce aviation fuel that meets applicable industry standards.

The project’s location near Saldanha Port is expected to support exports to international aviation markets, particularly in Europe and the United Kingdom. Regulatory requirements for lower carbon aviation fuels are expected to increase demand for e SAF ahead of 2030.

Phelan Green Group has also secured a long term off-taker agreement for the project. This provides an important commercial foundation by giving the facility a committed market for its production.

The remaining five projects in South Africa’s first wave of priority green hydrogen developments will continue to receive government support as they work towards their own final investment decisions. The projects cover green ammonia, green methanol corridors and green steel.

text:
Ecostrat Inc. and the BDO Zone Initiative are pleased to recognize the inclusion of Provectus Biofuels’ Vegreville Project in the Government of Canada’s Canada Investment Summit Prospectus. The proposed sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) facility sits within the Vegreville BDO Zone, which holds an investment grade ‘A’ Rating for wheat straw, and shows how a BDO Zone rating can carry a rural bio-based project onto a national investment stage.

Prime Minister Mark Carney is hosting the inaugural summit with CPP Investments and PSP Investments, bringing global investors to Toronto in support of Canada’s goal to catalyse $1 trillion in investment over five years. The summit prospectus presents 167 projects across eight sectors, from energy and critical minerals to digital technology and transportation, and lists the Vegreville Project under Clean Energy.

The facility would convert approximately 300,000 tonnes of agricultural straw into 75 million litres of SAF each year, at an estimated capital cost of US$450 million to US$600 million. The low-risk ‘A’ rating is issued for a surplus of 455,000 bone dry tonnes per year of wheat straw, and signals strong feedstock supply and infrastructure attributes. The rating was a major supporting factor in Provectus’ decision to locate in Vegreville.

“The investors in Toronto this week will ask the same question about any biofuel plant: where does the feedstock come from, and will it still be there in year fifteen? Vegreville answered that question before Provectus chose the site. Seeing this project in front of the world’s largest capital providers is the job BDO Zones were built to do, and Canada has room for many more of them,” stated Jordan Solomon, Chairman of the BDO Zone Initiative.

Canada now has 19 BDO Zones, part of a network of 73 across North America. In its April 2026 final report, the Canadian Forest Sector Transformation Task Force named the national scale-up of BDO Zone designation as a priority action. CSA Group and ASTM International have also signed a binational agreement to develop Biomass Supply Chain Risk (BSCR) and BDO Zone Assessment standards, giving investors a common benchmark for biomass supply on both sides of the border.

title: Heathrow expansion 'not compatible' with UK climate targets, government warned - News
description:
Aviation is one of the most difficult sectors to decarbonise, and Heathrow, one of the world’s busiest airports, already contributes to around half of the UK’s aviation emissions.
The CCC said 56% of the required emissions reductions from aviation could be met by industry-funded SAF and GGR technology.
Research fellow Lois Pennington said: “Sustainable aviation fuels and carbon removals can contribute to limiting aviation emissions, but there is currently no evidence that these technologies can support the scale of aviation expansion envisaged by the government.
Heathrow expansion is not currently compatible with the UK’s net zero target.
That’s why it’s so important the right policies are put in place now to fully address aviation emissions.”
text:
Philip Lange / Shutterstock.com

PLANS to expand London Heathrow Airport are “not compatible” with climate targets, an official panel has warned the government, unless the aviation industry pays for greater uptake of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and greenhouse gas removal (GGR) technology.

Heathrow won government backing for a third runway last year, but the Climate Change Committee (CCC), which advises the UK government on greenhouse gas emissions and sets the country’s legally binding carbon budgets, said there was currently “insufficient policy to decarbonise the UK aviation sector”, even without the planned expansion. The report comes after government-commissioned analysis found that expansion would have “significant adverse environmental effects”, even taking into account the possible growth of SAF and GGR technology.

Aviation is one of the most difficult sectors to decarbonise, and Heathrow, one of the world’s busiest airports, already contributes to around half of the UK’s aviation emissions. While most sectors will be “well advanced in their decarbonisation journey”, the CCC expects annual UK aviation emissions to climb from its current 37m tCO2e to 39m tCO2e by 2050 under existing policy – above the carbon budget limit of 37.5m tCO2e. A fully expanded Heathrow would generate an additional 4.5m tCO2e each year by 2054 on top of the 11.3m tCO2e predicted from construction of the new runway.

The CCC said 56% of the required emissions reductions from aviation could be met by industry-funded SAF and GGR technology. The remainder would need to come from demand reduction and efficiency improvements. At Heathrow alone, demand is expected to increase from 299m annual passengers currently to 474m by 2050. A third runway would increase this further to 491m.

The report acknowledged that the costs of SAF and GGR would likely make flight tickets more expensive. Tim Alderslade, CEO of Airlines UK, accused the CCC’s approach of “putting holidays out of reach for millions and turning the clock back to a time when flying was the preserve of the rich.” The CCC noted that currently around half of England’s population takes fewer than one flight a year.

Alderslade added: “Both SAF and GGRs are proven technically viable, as the CCC itself admits. We should focus on delivering them, not pricing ordinary people out of the joys of travel.”

However, a paper published last week by researchers at the University of Manchester-based Tyndall Centre and commissioned by Friends of the Earth warned there was no evidence the SAF and GGR industries were on track to reach the scales required to reach net zero by 2050. Research fellow Lois Pennington said: “Sustainable aviation fuels and carbon removals can contribute to limiting aviation emissions, but there is currently no evidence that these technologies can support the scale of aviation expansion envisaged by the government. Further aviation expansion carries a significant risk of exacerbating climate impacts by relying on the growth of technologies that are unlikely to materialise in the timescale needed.”

The CCC report also reflected the uncertainty in SAF and GGR and urged the government to develop “contingency policies” to account for delays in the technologies’ uptake. Only 1% of the required emissions reductions from GGR “are supported by credible plans”, the committee noted, while existing policy mandating 10% of all jet fuel to be SAF by 2030 is “insufficient”. Analysis by the European Federation for Transport & Environment last year found that European aviation emissions will continue increasing well into the 2040s even if the level of SAF uptake predicted by airlines is realised.

CCC chair Nigel Topping said: “Our advice is clear. Heathrow expansion is not currently compatible with the UK’s net zero target. Government needs to ensure that the aviation industry takes responsibility for the emissions it creates and bears the costs of decarbonisation. Those conditions do not exist today.

“This summer’s extreme weather has brought the impacts of climate change into sharp focus. Every tonne of greenhouse gas emissions makes those impacts worse. That’s why it’s so important the right policies are put in place now to fully address aviation emissions.”

description:
The Senate Agriculture Committee on Sept. 16 voted 12-11 to advance the Agriculture Act of 2026, commonly referred to as Senate Farm Bill 2.0.
With Senate Ag Committee approval, the Farm Bill 2.0 can now be considered by the full Senate.
The current Farm Bill is set to expire at the end of September.
The Renewable Fuels Association applauded committee passage of Farm Bill 2.0.
"Today’s passage of the farm bill by the Senate Agriculture Committee represents an important step toward finally securing nationwide, year-round E15," said Geoff Cooper, president and CEO of the RFA.
text:
The Senate Agriculture Committee on Sept. 16 voted 12-11 to advance the Agriculture Act of 2026, commonly referred to as Senate Farm Bill 2.0. The legislation includes provisions allowing year-round sales of E15 and supporting the sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) industry.

The vote to advanced Farm Bill 2.0 follows a failed attempt by the committee to advance the bill in early August when efforts were stalled by partisan divisions over food assistance provisions. Rather than adjuring the committee after that failed vote, Committee Chairman John Boozman, R-Ark., recessed the committee, a decision that allowed him to call committee members back to revisit the bill at a later date.

With Senate Ag Committee approval, the Farm Bill 2.0 can now be considered by the full Senate. No date has yet been set for a Senate vote on the legislative package. The current Farm Bill is set to expire at the end of September.

One provision of the Senate Farm Bill would enable year-round sales of E15 and implement reform to the Renewable Fuel Standard’s small refinery exemption (SRE) program.

In addition to E15 and SRE reform, the Senate Farm Bill’s energy title includes numerous provisions to support the U.S. biofuel industry, including major updates to the USDA’s Section 9003 loan guarantee program, language supporting the SAF industry, and the reauthorization of numerous bioenergy programs, including the Bioenergy Program for Advanced Biofuels, Biodiesel Fuel Education Program, Feedstock Flexibility Program for Bioenergy Producers, the Biomass Crop Assistance Program, and the Carbon Utilization and Biogas Education Program.

The Renewable Fuels Association applauded committee passage of Farm Bill 2.0. "Today’s passage of the farm bill by the Senate Agriculture Committee represents an important step toward finally securing nationwide, year-round E15," said Geoff Cooper, president and CEO of the RFA. "We thank Sen. Boozman and the members of the committee for ensuring the E15 provisions were included. As expressed throughout the farm bill process, there is broad bipartisan support for making lower-cost E15 available to consumers all year long—especially at a time when pump prices are on the rise and fuel supplies are tightening. Now, we urge the full Senate to pass year-round E15 legislation as quickly as possible, reconcile the language with the House, and get a viable solution to President Trump’s desk for his signature."

title: Transport NGOs call EU ETS aviation extension proposals a missed opportunity
description:
Meanwhile, a report from another European NGO, Opportunity Green, in collaboration with research consultancy CE Delft, finds European airlines received a cumulative €10.9 billion ($12.5bn) in free EU ETS allowances between 2013 and 2025.
Opportunity Green accuses the airlines of not lowering ticket prices as a result or contributing sufficiently to decarbonisation spending.
T&E calls on them to support an EU ETS extension to all departing flights and as of 2028, rather than the proposed 2029.
Opportunity Green said the Commission’s proposals represented a missed opportunity by exempting major markets like the US and China and leaving the most polluting long-haul flights with no incentive to decarbonise.
New analysis from Opportunity Green and CE Delft shows 350 million free EU ETS allowances were handed to airlines between 2013 and 2025, which they value at €10.9 billion.
text:
Analysis by Brussels-based NGO Transport & Environment (T&E) shows the recently released proposal from the European Commission to extend the scope of the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) to all departing flights to airports within 5,000km of Frankfurt from 2029 would cover around 59% of Europe’s departing aviation emissions, up from 44% today. It says SAF allowances will offset part of the increase, reducing the proportion of priced emissions to 57%. Meanwhile, a report from another European NGO, Opportunity Green, in collaboration with research consultancy CE Delft, finds European airlines received a cumulative €10.9 billion ($12.5bn) in free EU ETS allowances between 2013 and 2025. Opportunity Green accuses the airlines of not lowering ticket prices as a result or contributing sufficiently to decarbonisation spending.

In July, the Commission published its assessment that the current emissions coverage of the CORSIA carbon offsetting scheme for international aviation was insufficient and recommended an extended scope of the EU ETS to third countries. The scope would include flights to countries such as Turkey and the Gulf states, whose carriers and airports are considered to have an unfair competitive advantage over their European counterparts on carbon pricing, but exclude countries like the US, India and China that have in the past opposed EU extraterritorial application of its flagship carbon scheme (see graphics below).

T&E described the extended scope proposal as a “half-hearted” step towards pricing extra-EEA international flights, although acknowledging it as “a pragmatic first step that protects European interests”.

It points out that with only an effective 57% coverage, nearly half of Europe’s departing aviation emissions still would not carry a carbon price and airlines, including those from third countries, would get financial support for buying sustainable aviation fuel.

The proposal will now be debated by the European Parliament and EU member states through the European Council before a final decision is reached. T&E calls on them to support an EU ETS extension to all departing flights and as of 2028, rather than the proposed 2029.

It welcomed the proposals to include in the EU ETS all private jet flights, many of which have been exempted up till now, and the introduction of free allowances for airlines that avoid creating warming contrails.

Opportunity Green said the Commission’s proposals represented a missed opportunity by exempting major markets like the US and China and leaving the most polluting long-haul flights with no incentive to decarbonise.

New analysis from Opportunity Green and CE Delft shows 350 million free EU ETS allowances were handed to airlines between 2013 and 2025, which they value at €10.9 billion. Six of Europe’s biggest airlines – Lufthansa Group, Ryanair, easyJet, IAG, Air France-KLM and Wizz Air – are calculated to have received €6 billion, while making a combined €21 billion in profit over the period. The report estimates they incurred €320 billion of climate costs, while spending only €1 billion on decarbonisation activities such as SAF and ground equipment electrification.

“These figures show the industry’s narrative about struggling to remain competitive is greatly overblown,” commented Tom Grylls, Director of Analytics at Opportunity Green, on a report by CE Delft entitled ‘Who benefits from free allocation in aviation?’. “In reality, they have enjoyed years of freebies and instead of funding climate action through new innovations in sustainable technology or SAF deployment, this money simply turned to profit and lined the airlines’ deep pockets.”

Opportunity Green says free allowances are an ineffective tool to tackle competitiveness and a barrier to progress on tackling climate change, and calls on the Commission to exclude free allowance allocations in future EU ETS revisions.

Added Carly Hicks, Chief Strategy and Impact Officer: “The history of free allowances tells us that if airlines aren’t compelled to act on decarbonisation, they won’t. Under the latest proposals, any allowances for aviation are conditional upon sustainability criteria, such as using alternative fuels or mitigating contrails. It’s crucial the Commission sticks to this pathway and ensures the criteria are ambitious, even if the industry ends up asking for more free allowances.”

The organisation also recommends airlines should be charged a fee unless they take action to avoid contrails and calls for the abolition of the EU Taxonomy or, alternatively, reformed to adopt a stronger definition of sustainability that excludes investments in fossil-fuelled aircraft.

text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator Jerry Moran (R-Kan.) – a member of the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition and Forestry – today applauded the Senate Agriculture Committee’s passage of the Farm Bill, which includes a number of key priorities to support Kansas agriculture. The legislation now heads to the full Senate for consideration.

“This is a critical step to advance a Farm Bill that provides certainty for farmers and ranchers in Kansas and across the nation,” said Sen. Moran. “The legislation secures several important priorities to benefit the agriculture community, including year-round E-15, modernized farm loan limits, strengthened conservation programs, expanded trade promotion and the permanent transfer of Food for Peace to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. When farmers and ranchers are successful, rural America is successful. I will continue working with my colleagues to get this Farm Bill across the finish line and to the President’s desk to be signed into law.”

Kansas priorities secured in the Senate Farm Bill:

Year-round E-15 sales – Sen. Moran has long supported the year-round sale of E-15, which will help grow markets for producers and lower prices at the pump for Kansans and Americans.

Bolstering the Conservation Reserve Program – Sen. Moran introduced the Conservation Reserve Program (CRP) Improvement and Flexibility Act to increase flexibility for livestock grazing on conservation land.

Increasing Farm Service Agency (FSA) loan limits – Better reflects lending conditions in farm country and modernizes loan limits to support the needs of farmers and ranchers.

Doubling funding for USDA trade promotion programs – Strengthens the ability of U.S. producers to market their products globally.

Food for Peace permanently transferred to USDA – Sen. Moran led an amendment that was approved during the markup, securing the inclusion of his legislation in the Farm Bill to permanently transfer administration of the Food for Peace program to USDA.

Rural Hospital Revitalization Act – Sen. Moran introduced this legislation to provide temporary zero percent interest loans for the construction or renovation of qualifying rural healthcare facilities.

Farm to Fly Act – Sen. Moran introduced this legislation to accelerate the production and development of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) through existing USDA programs to allow further growth for alternative fuels to be used in the aviation sector and create new markets for American farmers.

Expanding career opportunities in agriculture for veterans – Sen. Moran’s Colonel Gary LaGrange AgVets Act establishes a USDA program to provide veterans with resources and opportunities to pursue careers in the agricultural industry.

In August, during initial committee consideration of the Farm Bill, Sen. Moran spoke about the importance of bipartisanship by members of the Senate Agriculture Committee to advance a Farm Bill that supports American farmers and ranchers. “My favorite people in the world are my farmers and ranchers and people who live in rural communities,” said Sen. Moran. “My favorite people in Congress are those who represent those kinds of people because we almost exclusively represent their values and their character and what they do for a living.”

“In the Senate and in Congress, there’s been these special places and the Committee on Agriculture has been one of them,” continued Sen. Moran. “And we ought to recommit ourselves. I think we need to reestablish the trust that this committee is about this committee’s work – and it’s not about the broader political implications that occur in all of our lives about who gets the majority next year after the election.”

“Developing Europe’s first dedicated sustainable aviation fuel facility is a major step in scaling SAF production and supporting aviation decarbonization,” said Bart Rosendaal, site director of DSL-01 at SkyNRG.
Emerson will also provide end-to-end project services, combining digital technologies and modern project management approaches to simplify engineering and optimise operations.

text:
Emerson has secured a contract from Technip Energies to supply automation technologies for SkyNRG’s sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) plant in Delfzijl, the first dedicated greenfield SAF production facility in Europe, Hydrocarbon Processing reported.

Emerson’s DeltaV integrated control and safety system (ICSS) will be deployed at the facility to support safe and reliable startup and long-term operations while helping reduce project risks.

Currently under construction, the facility is expected to begin operations in 2028 with an annual SAF production capacity of around 100,000 tonnes. The plant will convert residual fats and greases into sustainable “drop-in” aviation fuel that can be blended with conventional jet fuel without modifications to aircraft or existing fuelling infrastructure.

The project will support the Netherlands’ efforts to meet the European Union’s SAF requirements under the ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation. The regulation requires jet fuel supplied at EU airports to contain at least 2% SAF from 2025, with the requirement increasing progressively to 70% by 2050.

“Developing Europe’s first dedicated sustainable aviation fuel facility is a major step in scaling SAF production and supporting aviation decarbonization,” said Bart Rosendaal, site director of DSL-01 at SkyNRG.

“Working with experienced partners like Technip Energies and Emerson helps ensure we can deliver a safe, reliable and future-ready plant from day one,” he added.

As a greenfield project, the facility will incorporate digital automation technologies from the beginning. Emerson’s ICSS will combine its DeltaV distributed control system with a DeltaV safety instrumented system to provide process control, safety shutdown and fire and gas detection capabilities.

The company will also deploy its AMS Device Manager plant asset management software to support commissioning and maintenance by providing device information, equipment health insights and diagnostics from intelligent field devices.

The automation systems will cover the plant’s major process units, including the hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids process used to produce SAF, an advanced feedstock pre-treatment unit and an on-site hydrogen plant based on Technip Energies’ proprietary high-efficiency steam methane reforming technology.

According to Emerson, integration of these systems will provide real-time operational visibility and support stable and consistent plant performance, with the aim of improving reliability and optimising throughput.

Emerson will also provide end-to-end project services, combining digital technologies and modern project management approaches to simplify engineering and optimise operations.

Integration of the ICSS with multiple modular production units is expected to simplify commissioning. DeltaV Electronic Marshalling with distributed CHARMs will reduce field wiring requirements while providing greater flexibility to accommodate design changes during the later stages of the project.

“Projects such as SkyNRG’s SAF facility represent the future of energy and sustainable fuels,” said Nathan Pettus, president of Emerson’s process systems and solutions business.

“With complex, first-of-a-kind plants, early engineering alignment and a fully integrated automation architecture are key to delivering predictable project outcomes and consistent operational performance over the long term,” he added.

text:
The United States has launched a new strategy to expand international demand for American biofuels, signaling that overseas markets will play a growing role in the sector's future.

Announced by US Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins at the 17th annual Growth Energy Biofuels Summit, the American Biofuels Trade Outlook centers on four priorities: increasing on-road ethanol blending, removing foreign restrictions on US biofuels, targeting high-impact markets, and shaping international aviation and maritime regulations.

The strategy arrives as US ethanol exports reached record levels. The country exported 2.18 billion gallons in 2025, up 13% from the previous record in 2024. Exports represented 13.3% of US production, making international demand an increasingly critical part of the market balance.

Despite these positive trends, further growth is not guaranteed. Many prospective markets protect domestic producers, restrict crop-based fuels, or lack the infrastructure needed to turn blending targets into consumption. The new outlook recognizes that biofuels' global role will depend as much on market access and regulatory treatment as on production and price.

What Are the Four Pillars of the American Biofuels Trade Outlook?

1. Increase On-Road Ethanol Blending

The first pillar combines two objectives: encouraging E10 adoption in new markets and stabilizing access to countries that already have E10 policies.

The USDA sees potential breakthrough markets in Latin America and growth opportunities in Southeast Asia. E10 offers an accessible route to significant new demand because it can generally be used in vehicles without the specialized equipment required for higher ethanol blends. It can also help importing countries in several ways:

Diversify fuel supplies

Reduce petroleum dependence

Meet octane requirements

At the same time, the USDA plans to address policy implementation challenges across approximately 20 existing E10 markets. Announced blending targets do not always translate into physical demand. Infrastructure gaps, inconsistent standards, delayed mandates, and difficult import procedures can all limit consumption.

This pillar seeks both expansion and stability: opening new markets while ensuring that established blending policies create reliable demand.

2. Remove Foreign Restrictions

The second pillar aims to challenge foreign policies that limit the use of US crop-based biofuels. The European Union is a particular focus because its treatment of crop-based fuels can restrict their contribution to transport decarbonization targets.

These rules matter beyond conventional road fuels. Restrictions tied to feedstocks or lifecycle greenhouse gas calculations can also affect whether US-produced fuels qualify for use in aviation and marine markets.

For the US, removing such barriers could broaden the range of applications available to corn- and soybean-based fuels. But this will require more than conventional trade promotion.

Many restrictions are embedded in climate and sustainability policy. Accordingly, US exporters must demonstrate both environmental performance and commercial competitiveness.

3. Target High-Impact Markets

The third pillar will deploy USDA market-access programs and the America First Trade Promotion Program to pursue strategic growth. India was highlighted as a potential market for on-road expansion, alongside Indonesia, Japan, and Vietnam.

The USDA is seeking access to a distinct and politically sensitive part of the Indian market. The same tension may emerge elsewhere: countries can value ethanol's energy-security benefits while using blending mandates to support domestic farmers and producers.

Federal trade programs may help build commercial relationships and address technical barriers. However, the largest gains will depend on whether target countries change policies that favor local supply.

4. Shape Global Regulations

The fourth pillar calls for greater US engagement with the International Civil Aviation Organization and the International Maritime Organization. The objective is to secure fair treatment for US biofuels as global aviation and shipping regulations evolve.

These sectors could become significant sources of low-carbon fuel demand because both are difficult to electrify. Access will depend on how international frameworks calculate lifecycle emissions, recognize different production pathways, and treat crop-based feedstocks.

More Insights on Aviation and Marine

Sustainable Aviation Fuel Monthly Snapshot

Bio-Bunkering at a Glance: Marine Biofuels Monthly Update

Lower-carbon farming practices, renewable process energy, and carbon capture could improve the position of US fuels. Their value in international markets, however, will depend on whether regulatory frameworks recognize those emissions reductions.

What Does the Strategy Mean for Biofuel Markets?

For US producers, the outlook confirms that exports are becoming structurally important. Domestic gasoline demand may offer limited long-term growth as vehicle efficiency improves and electrification advances. International blending programs provide another outlet for producers and, indirectly, for US corn and soybean growers.

Additionally, current economic strains between Iran and the US have placed added pressure on domestic fuel markets, driving average fuel costs to record levels. These considerations have made the calls for alternative fuel sources, including biofuels, a much larger part of the conversation.

Globally, the strategy reflects biofuels’ evolution from primarily domestic policy tools into more widely traded energy commodities. Yet the market will not become fully open. Governments will continue to balance competitively priced imports against domestic agricultural, energy-security, and industrial priorities.

Competition will increasingly extend beyond price. Market share will also depend on verified carbon intensity, reliable supply, and compatibility with national and international rules. The outlook's emphasis on both trade barriers and global regulation reflects that shift.

Market Access Will Determine the Outcome

The American Biofuels Trade Outlook identifies four credible routes to growth. But its commercial effect will depend on measurable policy changes and physical trade.

The outlook serves as an important statement of intent, not a guarantee of demand. Its progress will show whether the US can convert record exports into a broader and more durable role for American biofuels in global energy markets.

text:
A leaked European Commission impact assessment working document for the upcoming Renewable Energy Directive, RED IV, signals a potentially significant shift in renewable fuels policy after 2030. The draft's "preferred pacage" would replace binding national renewable hydrogen mandates with a more flexible EU-wide target, while giving greater room to crop-based biofuels and favoring advanced biofuels made from European feedstocks. The direction suggests that energy security, cost and national flexibility are gaining weight alongside emissions reduction, although the measures remain subject to change before the Commission publishes its formal proposal.

For hydrogen, the working document outlines three policy pathways for the post-2030 period. RED III currently anchors demand through binding national mandates, including a renewable fuels of non-biological origin (RFNBOs) target of 1% in transport by 2030 and RFNBO shares of 42% in industry by 2030 and 60% by 2035. Under the preferred RED IV option, these obligations would be replaced by an indicative EU-wide renewable hydrogen consumption target for industry and refineries of 8 million tonnes. The assessment describes the 8 million tonnes as the “average optimal level for the period covered by the policy,” which industry reporting has interpreted as the annual consumption by 2040. The preferred pathway envisages hydrogen credits and downstream demand incentives, which would need to be implemented through other legislation.

Rystad Energy’s base case sees total EU green hydrogen demand reaching 9.5 million tonnes by 2040. If the draft’s 8 million tonnes figure is interpreted as annual consumption in 2040, it would represent a large share of total forecast demand, particularly given that the indicative target applies only to industry and refineries. This suggests that the headline volume itself may be less important than the question of how the target would ultimately be delivered.

“For Europe’s hydrogen market, the prospect of replacing binding national obligations adds another layer of policy uncertainty at a time when projects still depend heavily on long-term demand visibility to secure offtake and reach final investment decisions. Production, infrastructure, and demand need to develop in parallel, and greater flexibility could help concentrate production in lower-cost regions. However, if long-term demand signals remain strong in only a few member states, the market risks developing in separate pockets rather than as an integrated European market. The key question is therefore whether the final framework can provide sufficiently strong and durable mechanisms to support demand if binding national obligations are replaced.”

- Frederick Andre Wessel, Product Manager of Hydrogen Research, Rystad Energy

For biofuels, the draft points in a more supportive direction, reflecting a stronger focus on energy security. A common 7% EU ceiling for crop-based biofuels could increase eligible conventional biofuel volumes by around 30% compared with the 2020 basis used in the assessment, while advanced biofuels produced from EU-sourced feedstocks could receive preferential treatment through multipliers. This would support efforts to reduce import dependence: the EU imported around 1.8 million tonnes of hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO) last year and more than half of its sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) supply.

The picture is less straightforward for advanced biofuels, as the draft assumes the existing combined transport minimum for advanced biofuels and RFNBOs expires after 2030, leaving demand more dependent on national policy. Stricter certification requirements could restrict some imported fuels and feedstocks, improving the competitive position of European producers. Overall, the draft points to diverging implications across renewable fuels: weaker policy certainty for hydrogen, but potentially stronger support for biofuels linked to domestic European resources.

By Rystad Energy

Under the Government of Canada’s proposed Productivity Mega Deduction, businesses could deduct the full cost of an eligible aircraft in the year it becomes available for use, instead of depreciating the aircraft over several years under the regular taxes.

Two requirements matter:

Acquired on or after Sept. 15, 2026

Available for use:The aircraft must be ready to fly for the business. If it is still being completed or refurbished at year-end, the deduction generally waits until it is ready for use.

Used aircraft can qualify, too, subject to specific rules. The aircraft cannot have previously been owned by the taxpayer or a non-arm’s-length person, and it cannot have been acquired through certain tax-deferred transfers.

“This is a significant advocacy win for CBAA and our members,” said Harlan Simpkins, president and CEO of CBAA. “We consistently strive for policies that drive investments and strengthen Canada’s competitiveness. Including aircraft in the Productivity Mega Deduction is a solid initiative for business aviation opportunities.”

“This announcement shows what we can achieve by unifying our voice and working together,” added Simpkins. “CBAA will continue working with government and our industry partners to ensure the vital contribution of business aviation is recognized in the policies that share our sector.”

CBAA will monitor the implementation of the new measure and keep members informed as further details become available.

Read the Government Announcement: Prime Minister Carney introduces new Productivity Mega Deduction.

This press release was prepared and distributed by the Canadian Business Aviation Association.

text:
Sasol has signed a first-of-its-kind agreement to supply co-processed sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) to White Desert, a luxury Antarctic expedition company.

The petrochemical company said the deal marks a significant milestone for African aviation and for South Africa’s emerging lower-carbon fuels industry.

"Enabled by Natref’s recent ISCC+ sustainability certification, the agreement reinforces the role South African industry can play in the global transition to lower-carbon energy."

Announced at the Africa Green Hydrogen Summit, the agreement will see Sasol’s first commercial SAF volumes supplied to White Desert for its Cape Town-to-Antarctica expeditions.

The SAF to be supplied is produced from sustainable bio-feedstocks and provides a stepping stone towards future e-fuels enabled by green hydrogen, Sasol said.

The fuel is produced from used cooking oil, explains Danie Cronje, Sasol senior vice president for Business Building.

"The input into the feedstock is used cooking oil that we aggregate from users in South Africa and co-process in our Natref refinery in Sasolburg. That then produces sustainable aviation fuel that we onsell to White Desert."

"That oil has got the same formula as general fossil fuels, just a different chemical composition, but essentially the same energy value. The plant can distill it and extract the right chemical formulation to produce the fuel spec that is required to fly the planes."

This particular fuel delivers a reduction of about 75% in carbon emissions, Cronje says.

Natref can produce around 1 to 2 million litres of sustainable air fuels at present, he says.

The refinery's capability is being ramped up, with the expectation that by the end of 2027 it will be able to produce 15 million litres, which will continue to rise.

As demand increases, they will also be scaling up their Secunda plant for this purpose.

Taking into consideration the modifications involved, SAF is overall around two to three times more expensive than conventional jet fuel, he says.

"For now, the target market is unique and boutique technology like White Desert that has a very clear ambition to be net zero. So we are matching customer demand with our production capability as we slowly scale up."

Cronje gives the assurance that, as the demand for SAF grows, Sasol will be there to supply that volume.

title: Heathrow third runway should only go ahead if the aviation sector cleans up its act, govt told

"Government needs to ensure the aviation industry takes responsibility for the emissions it creates and bears the costs of decarbonisation.

text:
The Climate Change Committee (CCC) on Wednesday (16 September) said there is "no credible pathway" for Heathrow to expand under the UK's current climate commitments.

“Our advice today is clear – Heathrow expansion is not currently compatible with the UK’s net zero target," said CCC Chair Nigel Topping. "Government needs to ensure the aviation industry takes responsibility for the emissions it creates and bears the costs of decarbonisation. Those conditions do not exist today."

While the CC has no power to block ministers from approving Heathrow's third runway – a vote in the House of Commons is expected later this year – it can advocate for the government to firm up the rules governing the speed at which aviation pursues decarbonisation.

The CC said the only way expansion could be achieved in a way that is consistent with the UK's current environmental targets would be for government to implement "a robust set of policies" requiring the aviation to achieve zero emissions by 2050.

It said this could yet be achieved through a combination of direct reductions in emissions, such as by reducing flying, and paying for carbon reduction technologies, although it also warns only 1% of engineered removals in its sixth carbon budget (2033 to 2037) are "supported by credible plans".

What is a carbon budget? And what does the latest one mean for travel?

The CC's report advocates for a net zero aviation pathway based on a "polluter pays" principle, which would see engineered removals account for reducing emissions by more than a third (36%) and lower demand growth by nearly a quarter (24%).

Efficiency improvements would account for another 20% and the rollout of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) for the final 20%. Under the CC's proposals, the aviation industry would pay for engineered removals and SAF.

However, it warns under this route, ticket prices for a return trip to Alicante could increase by around £150 by 2050 and a return New York trip by £400.

The CC's key asks of government include:

Requiring the aviation industry to fund the full cost of decarbonisation "no later than 2050", adding these measures need to be phased in "starting soon";

Factoring in contingencies should it prove more difficult than first thought to engineer emission removals and deploy SAF at scale;

Ensuring, if expansion is permitted, any commercial risks associated with future aviation demand sits with investors, not consumers; and

Ensuring too that the burden doesn't fall on taxpayers; "those who do not fly should not face these costs" it said in its latest Carbon Budget (2038 to 2042)

According to the CC, emissions from aviation have more than doubled since 1990, during which time emissions across the UK economy as a whole have halved.

'Work with us' plea to government

Karen Dee, Chief Executive of AirportsUK, said the aviation sector was well aware of the decarbonisation work still needing to be done if it is to expand.

"It is essential that this is delivered in a way which protects UK competitiveness and that the considerable sums consumers are already being asked to pay are better used to support decarbonisation," said Dee.

“Industry has a credible plan to decarbonise by 2050 taking into account growth through expansion, through sustainable aviation fuel, airspace modernisation, more efficient aircraft and other measures. The government’s focus should be to work with the sector to ensure its policy framework supports this plan.”

Tim Alderslade, Chief Executive of Airlines UK, said airlines were supportive of net zero by 2050 but stressed the transition had to be affordable. "Airlines are already investing billions in new aircraft, SAF and airspace upgrades and we have a plan to deliver it.

"The CCC's approach would add £600 to a family's trip to Europe and £1,600 to New York by 2050, putting holidays out of reach for millions and turning the clock back to a time when flying was the preserve of the rich. You can't solve the climate crisis by pricing Britain out of the skies.

"The answer is affordable SAF – already cutting emissions since the mandate began – airspace reform by 2035 for more direct routes and scaled-up carbon removals. Both SAF and GGRs [greenhouse gas removals] are proven technically viable, as the CCC itself admits. We should focus on delivering them, not pricing ordinary people out of the joys of travel."

Duncan McCourt, Chief Executive of Sustainable Aviation, said the UK's aviation sector was making "real progress" on decarbonisation, claiming per passenger emissions have gone down by 22% since 2005 amid a near-30% increase in passenger numbers.

"Behind the headline of the CCC report, there is much we agree on: UK aviation can continue to grow and still reach net zero by 2050. To do that, stronger policies and international cooperation are needed.

"We strongly disagree with the CCC conclusion that aviation should not be able to expand until the full framework of policies to decarbonise are in place. That is like saying we shouldn’t build any new homes or cars or produce any steel, cement or chemicals until decarbonisation policies are finished.

"Expansion of an industry can, and should, go hand-in-hand with the development and implementation of policy to decarbonise.”
